title: POC weekly sync - Dedicated sizing
summary: Weekly POC sync to review recent benchmark results on Dedicated nodes, discuss autoscaling policy and burst handling, and align on next steps for pilot validation and SLOs.
action_items: Priya Singh: run 3-hour load test with 10k concurrent tokens/min and share logs (due: 2026-07-10)
Jordan Patel: provide updated autoscale config recommendation and sample HPA manifest (due: 2026-07-09)
Maya Chen: share pricing estimate for burst addon and reserved slots (due: 2026-07-08)
next_steps: Customer to run extended throughput test and upload results to shared drive
Redwood to propose autoscale policy and pre-warm script
Schedule technical deep dive with SREs next Wednesday
Redwood to share SOC 2 scoping doc and dedicated sizing spreadsheet
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-06 15:00 UTC | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - StratusHealth), Marcus Reed (SRE), Priya Singh (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we have Jordan and me from Redwood. Lena, Marcus, Priya from Stratus?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: Yep that's right, thanks Maya. Running a bit late on the last run so appreciate the time.
[00:12] Marcus Reed: Morning / afternoon all, Marcus here.
[00:15] Priya Singh: Hi all, Priya.
[00:18] Jordan Patel: Cool. Agenda — review last week's benchmark (we saw p95 spikes on long seqs), discuss autoscale tuning and burst capacity, and agree on next steps. Any additions?
[00:30] Lena Ortiz: No, that's it. We're mostly focused on ensuring we won't hit outages during peak ingestion windows.

Summary: The team walked through the dedicated sizing results; observed steady throughput for 2 million tokens/hour on a pool of 4x A10G nodes but saw p99 latency jumps when many long-context requests hit concurrently. Jordan proposed an autoscaling policy combining target CPU/GPU util with request queue length, and a burst pool of 2 reserved slots for sudden spikes. Action items were assigned: Redwood to propose concrete autoscale config and pre-warm scripts; customer to run extended stress test.

[05:00] Jordan Patel: Quick walk-through of the numbers — so with 4x A10G-ish nodes (we prototyped on g4/ g5 equivalent), baseline throughput for short requests (~128 tokens) is around 9k rps cumulative, or about 2M tokens/hour. But when you throw in long sequences (2k tokens) the KV cache pressure and attention compute causes latency to climb — we saw p99 hitting 3.2 seconds in that run.
[05:38] Priya Singh: Right, that p99 is concerning because our SLA target for interactive scoring is 500ms. The majority of our traffic is short, but we have periodic batch jobs and clinician notes ingestion that are large.
[05:52] Marcus Reed: Also worth flagging we saw cold-start-ish anomalies when a new replica spun up; the weights/prefetch seemed slower, maybe the warm cache isn't populated quickly.
[06:05] Jordan Patel: Yeah, that's the KV cache warm-up — on Dedicated we recommend either pre-warming or a short ramp policy. If you have a queue-length trigger we can spin up replicas early to avoid p99 spikes.

[10:00] Lena Ortiz: Can you explain the queue-length trigger? How does that differ from autoscale on GPU util?
[10:12] Jordan Patel: Sure. GPU util alone can be noisy because with LLMs a single long request can saturate a GPU for seconds while util averages out. Queue-length (or pending requests per instance) gives you a better signal for latency pressure. Our recommended policy is a hybrid: scale when GPU util > 70% for 2 minutes OR pending queue > 8 requests per instance for 30s. Also a hard cap to avoid runaway scale.
[10:42] Priya Singh: Makes sense — will that play nice with batching? We rely on batching for cost efficiency.
[10:49] Jordan Patel: Yes — we respect batching, the scheduler will attempt to batch across in-flight requests; but if queue builds up, scale happens to add more capacity so batches don't become huge and increase latency.

[15:00] Marcus Reed: About burst handling — we had a spike during last Tuesday's import window. What's the recommended approach: burst pool vs auto-burst?
[15:12] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we offer a reserved burst pool (configurable). Idea: keep N reserved slots that are kept warm via minimal traffic (heartbeat) so they can absorb short-lived spikes. There's also a paid burst addon where Redwood can provision temporary GPU capacity from a shared pool in your region.
[15:36] Lena Ortiz: If we reserve 2 slots, that costs extra, right? We need numbers to justify.
[15:42] Maya Chen: Yes we'll share pricing. I'll include a line item for 2 reserved A10G-equivalent slots and the burst addon pricing in the estimate.

[20:00] Jordan Patel: Technical note — pre-warm script: we recommend issuing a small forward pass (100-200 tokens) on startup to populate KV cache and JIT the kernels. We can provide a sample script for your infra (we tested a shell+curl example and a python async client). That reduces the cold start tail by about 60% in our tests.
[20:25] Priya Singh: Please send that. Also curious about sequence length routing — can we route long-context requests to a model variant that's optimized/quantized to handle longer contexts?
[20:36] Jordan Patel: Yep that's a common pattern. Smart routing rule: if expected tokens > 1k, route to a high-memory variant with higher throughput per token but slightly higher cost. We'll include a sample routing policy in the doc.

[25:00] Lena Ortiz: On security/compliance, Marcus had a question about audit log retention for Dedicated.
[25:08] Marcus Reed: Yes — we need 13 months of request-level audit logs for our internal audit. Is that supported on Private/Dedicated?
[25:15] Maya Chen: Dedicated supports configurable log retention; for hosted we'll need to check the retention tiers. For Private we can meet longer retention since data stays in your VPC. I'll attach the SOC2/logging doc.
[25:33] Marcus Reed: Great. Also, KMS integration — we need to ensure model keys are in our HSM for the pilot.
[25:42] Jordan Patel: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Dedicated/Private; some initial config is required but it's in the standard onboarding checklist.

[30:00] Priya Singh: Back to sizing: do you have a recommended formula to convert tokens/sec to GPUs for mixed workloads?
[30:10] Jordan Patel: Simple heuristic: determine your steady-state token/sec for short requests and peak token/sec for long requests. For short-requests-heavy workloads, x tokens/sec per A10G ~ 600 tokens/sec for generative workloads at 128 token context. For long requests (2k tokens) the per-GPU throughput drops; plan for 30-40% lower effective tps. Add a buffer of 20% for headroom. Example: your steady is 5k tokens/sec -> 9 A10G nodes; with long request mix you might need 11-12.
[30:45] Lena Ortiz: Ok that's helpful. Our telemetry shows steady ~3200 tokens/sec with spikes to 9k for 10-15 minutes. So maybe 6-7 nodes steady + 2 reserved burst makes sense.

[35:00] Marcus Reed: On autoscale cooldowns — what cooldowns do you recommend to avoid flapping?
[35:08] Jordan Patel: Use a 2-minute upscale cool-down and a 5-7 minute downscale cooldown. Also use scale stabilization policy (choose to wait for X consecutive samples) so you don't flip-flop on transient noise.
[35:25] Priya Singh: Do we need to change batch sizes during scale events?
[35:29] Jordan Patel: Batching adapts, but we have per-instance batch size caps. Typically you can keep same batch target and let scheduler split when more instances come up.

[40:00] Lena Ortiz: Any notes on observability we should enable during the pilot?
[40:08] Maya Chen: Enable token-level metrics, per-route latency, queue-length, GPU util, and KV cache hit rate. We'll share a dashboard template. Also instrument synthetic warm-up traffic before peak windows.
[40:25] Marcus Reed: We'll add those to our telemetry.

Recap and next steps:
[42:00] Maya Chen: Quick recap — Redwood will: 1) share autoscale config and HPA manifest example, 2) provide pre-warm script and routing policy example, 3) send pricing estimate for 2 reserved slots and burst addon, 4) attach SOC2/logging doc. Stratus will: 1) run extended 3-hour throughput test and upload logs, 2) confirm token/sec steady-state and spike windows, 3) align SREs for deep dive next Wed.
[43:10] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. Thx all.
[43:14] Priya Singh: I'll start the test tonight and aim to have results by Friday.
[43:20] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invite for the SRE deep dive.

[46:30] Meeting end.

Notes: Transcription includes minor mis-hearings, 'A10G' sometimes labeled as 'A1OG' in the raw export, and 'KV cache' occasionally appears as 'K V cash'.
